query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a post-solidification severe plastic deformation process—such as high-pressure torsion (HPT)—to refine the dual-phase lamellar colony spacing and improve interlamellar bond integrity in eutectic high-entropy alloys will simultaneously enhance room-temperature tensile strength and ductility compared to the conventional processing route.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies featuring numerous internal boundaries and coarse interlamellar spacing that facilitates microcrack nucleation during tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Subject the as-solidified eutectic alloy to high-pressure torsion processing under controlled conditions to induce severe plastic deformation, refine the lamellar spacing, and improve the chemical and mechanical integrity of the colony interfaces.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation tests carried out on samples processed via conventional routes versus those post-processed by HPT.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined lamellar spacing and enhanced interlamellar bonding at the colony boundaries, leading to a more uniform load distribution and delayed microcrack initiation.
generation.mechanism: HPT-induced grain refinement increases strength via the Hall–Petch effect while the improved cohesion and reduced spacing at colony interfaces reduce stress concentrations and microcrack initiation, thereby enhancing ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified lamellar colonies, HPT-processed samples will exhibit higher tensile strength and improved elongation at fracture, reflecting a beneficial shift in the strength–ductility balance.
generation.baseline: Conventionally processed eutectic HEA with coarse dual-phase lamellar colonies that trade off ductility for strength, with early microcrack initiation leading to brittle failure.
generation.boundary: The intervention is effective if the HPT processing is optimized to achieve uniform lamellar refinement without introducing excessive processing defects or promoting the formation of detrimental secondary phases; results may vary if processing parameters fall outside the optimal deformation range.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of strength and ductility enhancement is uncertain and will depend on the precise HPT parameters (e.g., pressure, number of revolutions) and the alloy composition; further experimental calibration is required to quantify these improvements.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples from the same ingot. Process one set conventionally and subject the other set to HPT under parameters optimized for lamellar refinement. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests coupled with microscopic examinations (SEM/TEM) to assess lamellar spacing and interfacial integrity. Compare the tensile strength, ductility, and microcrack initiation sites between the two sets.
measurements: Tensile strength and elongation at fracture via standard tensile tests
Lamellar spacing and interlamellar bonding quality via SEM/TEM
Fracture surface morphology to detect microcrack origins
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HPT-processed samples do not show statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility (or if they exhibit similar or worse performance relative to the conventionally processed samples), or if microstructural analysis does not confirm a refined lamellar structure with improved interfacial integrity, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: How do different powder metallurgy processing routes (CIP, sintering, HIP, swaging, SPS, HPT) affect the microstructure, oxygen content, porosity, and mechanical properties of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr high entropy alloy?. System: HfNbTaTiZr (equiatomic) high entropy alloy. Processing: Three initial powder types were used: (1) Elemental powders mixed for 10 h at 45 rpm and cold isostatically pressed (CIP) at 400 MPa; (2) Mechanical alloying (MA) via high energy ball milling for 42 h; (3) Gas atomized (AT) powder. Subsequent routes included sintering at 1400 °C for 16 h, HIP at 1400 °C/190 MPa for 2 h, hot swaging at 950 °C (with and without Ti-alloy envelope), Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 1300 °C/80 MPa for 2 min, and High Pressure Torsion (HPT) at 2.5 GPa for 15 revolutions.. Test conditions: Vickers hardness measured with 98.1 N load; microstructure analyzed via LM, SEM (BSE), and XRD; oxygen content determined by gas fusion; porosity via SEM image analysis; dislocation density via positron lifetime spectroscopy.. Paper card. Question: How does an ultrafine-grain microstructure, obtained via stationary friction processing, affect the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy?. System: Equimolar AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Stationary friction processing (SFP) using a WC-cylindrical tool (12 mm diameter) at rotational speeds of 400 rpm and 1800 rpm for 5 min duration. Test conditions: Isothermal oxidation in laboratory air at 850, 950, and 1050 °C for 100 h.
